claims.text: A defect- and oxygen-inclusive framework will predict temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The relevant bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains intrinsic microstructural defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
CPA provides a quantum-mechanical treatment of substitutionally disordered solid solutions.
Combining electronic-structure calculations with machine-learning-based corrections can account for defect-associated local atomic relaxations.
Defect and impurity scattering predominantly controls carrier mobility in HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering couples with oxygen-induced effects in HfNbTaTiZr at approximately 300–1200 K.
Microstructural defects and interstitial oxygen perturb the local atomic and electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly incorporating defects and oxygen modifies the computed electronic band structure and carrier-scattering rates.
More realistic band structures and scattering rates will make the calculations mirror measured conduction behavior more closely.
The enhanced model will achieve conductivity errors of approximately ±10–15% in both specified temperature regimes.
Conventional perfect-crystal conductivity models have errors exceeding 20% for this material.
Existing analytical conductivity models assume defect-free crystals and neglect scattering from microstructural defects and oxygen.
The proposed model is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing oxygen near 1 wt.% and temperatures of 0–200 K or 300–1200 K.
Performance outside the stated oxygen content and temperature intervals is untested.
The error reduction and robustness across defect-density regimes depend on defect characterization and calibration-data quality.
Four-probe conductivity measurements at 50, 150, 600, and 1100 K can test the proposed model against conventional models.
Defect density and oxygen distribution can be characterized using TEM or atom-probe tomography.
Failure to achieve ±10–15% conductivity error or to outperform the conventional model in either temperature regime falsifies the hypothesis.
